title: The Power of Words and Friends
overview: This chapter is a collection of short sayings, most of them about how our words, our pride and our relationships can build a life up or wreck it.

parts.label: The self-absorbed fool (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: These sayings picture someone who cuts himself off to chase his own wants and would rather air his opinions than understand anything. Wrongdoing, they add, brings scorn and disgrace with it.

parts.label: Words that harm or heal (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Wise speech is pictured as deep water and a fresh, running stream, though scholars read verse 4 in slightly different ways. The rest warns against siding with the guilty in court, against careless talk that drags a fool into fights, and against gossip, which goes down like a tasty snack and lodges deep inside.

parts.label: Where real safety lies (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Being slack at work is as damaging as wasting things outright. The LORD's name, meaning who God has shown himself to be, is a strong tower to run into, while the rich only imagine their money is a high wall, and pride comes just before a fall.

parts.label: Listen before you judge (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Answering before hearing someone out is foolish, and the first side of a story sounds right until the other side is questioned. Verse 16 notes that a gift can open doors to powerful people, and readers differ on whether it is a plain observation or a quiet warning about bribes.

parts.label: Disputes and the tongue (vv. 18-21)
parts.note: Casting lots, a bit like drawing straws, settled hard arguments, and the result was seen as in God's hands, while a wronged relative can be harder to win back than a walled city. Words carry the power of life and death, so people live with the results of what they say.

parts.label: Wife, poor, and true friends (vv. 22-24)
parts.note: A man who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favor from the LORD, while the poor must plead and the rich answer harshly. The first line of verse 24 is unclear in Hebrew, so translations differ on what it says about friends, but the second line speaks of a friend closer than a brother, whom Christians have often read as pointing to Jesus.

think: When has hearing the other side of a story changed how you saw someone?
